one_liner: Four-file C library for training small MLPs, CNNs and RNNs on CPU; beat 2017 Theano+Keras and tiny-dnn in its own runs.
what_it_does: KANN builds a static computational graph of tensor operators (dense, conv1d/conv2d, max pooling, dropout, GRU/LSTM/vanilla RNN layers, several cost functions) and trains it with graph-based reverse-mode automatic differentiation. The API is plain C: build nodes with kann_layer_* and kad_* calls, compile with kann_new(), then train with kann_train_fnn1() or a hand-written loop around kann_cost() and kann_RMSprop(), and predict with kann_apply1(). RNNs are trained by unrolling them to a fixed length with kann_unroll(). It is not a drop-in for Keras, TensorFlow or tiny-dnn; models are saved in KANN's own binary format.
how_it_is_fast: There is little framework overhead: one C graph evaluated in topological order with float32 buffers, no interpreter or Python layer. Matrix products use a cache-tiled sgemm built on hand-written 4-wide SSE (or, since June 2025, NEON) sdot/saxpy kernels, or cblas_sgemm when compiled with HAVE_CBLAS (OpenBLAS gave the README's fastest rows). Convolution is direct computation with an optimized inner loop and an NCHW-to-NHWC reshuffle, not im2col, so it needs little working memory but does not benefit from BLAS. Multi-threading (kann_mt) splits each mini-batch across cloned networks on pthreads and averages their gradients, which scaled better than the 2017 Theano+Keras setup.
when_to_use: Training or running small to medium networks (an MLP with tens to hundreds of hidden units, a small CNN, a two-layer GRU of 160 units) inside a C or C++ program without Python, CUDA or a framework dependency.
Embedding a trainable model in a tool where the four source files (kann.c, kann.h, kautodiff.c, kautodiff.h, about 3,900 lines) can be vendored, for example bioinformatics or command-line utilities.

CPU-only multi-core training of tiny models where per-step framework overhead dominates and intra-batch threading across 4 cores helps (the README's 4-thread rows beat Theano+Keras by about 1.3x to 2.4x, derived from page data).
Building non-standard graphs (shared weights, multiple inputs, outputs or costs, VAEs, recurrent nodes) in C when tiny-dnn's layer stack is too rigid.
Learning how a reverse-mode autodiff engine and RNN unrolling work; the code and doc/02dev.md are short enough to read in an afternoon.
when_not_to_use: Anything that needs GPUs, large networks or modern operators: no GPU backend, no batch normalization, no attention or transformer layers, float32 only.

Single-threaded convolution or RNN training without BLAS: KANN's own kernels lost to MKL-backed Theano+Keras in the README (mnist-cnn 57m57s vs 37m12s, mul100-rnn 40m05s vs 27m30s), and doc/02dev.md says its direct convolution is about twice as slow as Theano's GEMM-based one.

When you need a maintained project: the only commits after April 2021 are two in June 2025 (NEON support and an mt-mode API), and issues such as #33 (mnist-cnn assert failure, 2019) and #34 (kann_class_error returns 0 for KANN_C_CEB, 2020) are still open.
Interchange with other frameworks: no ONNX or Keras import/export, only kann_save/kann_load in its own format.
Wide-SIMD x86 targets where you expect AVX2/AVX-512 or FMA: the built-in kernels are 128-bit SSE intrinsics; link OpenBLAS (make CBLAS=...) to get faster dense layers.

integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and libm; optional pthreads (HAVE_PTHREAD, on in the Makefile) and an optional CBLAS such as OpenBLAS (HAVE_CBLAS); the examples' kann_extra/kann_data.c uses zlib
integration.min_toolchain: ANSI C / C89-compatible compiler (README; the Makefile builds with gcc -O2 and also checks -Wc++-compat); kann.h has extern "C" guards for C++
integration.platforms: any C target; SSE fast path on x86-64, NEON fast path on aarch64 since June 2025, scalar fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Not documented as thread-safe. One kann_t must not be used from several threads; kann_mt() runs its own worker threads that main-thread code busy-waits on, and the default random number state (kad_rand(0), kann_srand) and kann_verbose are unsynchronized globals.

gotchas: Harness differences behind the README table (none invalidates it, but the rows are not like-for-like): KANN's mnist-cnn adds two dropout(0.2) layers that the Keras (-C without -d) and tiny-dnn models lack; the TensorFlow script trains with Adam and tiny-dnn with plain SGD and softmax cross-entropy, while KANN and Keras use RMSprop with sigmoid binary cross-entropy; the Python scripts print their own timers (Keras rnn-bit.py includes model build and Theano compilation, mlp.py excludes it) while the KANN examples have no internal timer, and the README does not say which timer produced each row; the scripts leave theano.config.openmp commented out, so Theano's 4-CPU rows thread only MKL GEMM.

examples/rnn-bit.c trains with 'for (j = 0; j < d->n - mini_size; j += mini_size)', so each epoch skips the tail of the data (468 batches, 29,952 of the 30,000 mul100 samples); the extra work this saves is under 0.2%, so it does not explain the RNN speedups.

kann_mt() synchronizes by spinning on a volatile int counter rather than atomics or a condition variable on the main thread: one core is burned while workers run, and the pattern relies on x86 memory ordering, a concern for the new aarch64 NEON build. The NEON kernels carry a source comment saying they were 'translated from SSE to NEON by LLM' and have no published benchmarks.

Issue #44 (Apple M1) reports the Getting Started rnn-bit example printing 1924146487037 instead of 1138429; the low 21 bits match and only bits 38-40 are wrong (derived from issue data), because rnn-bit's apply mode decodes 64 steps while the model was trained on the data's bit length, so untrained steps can emit spurious 1s. Also, the examples call kad_trap_fe(), which unmasks SSE invalid and divide-by-zero exceptions, so an invalid operation (a NaN-producing step) or a division by zero makes them crash with SIGFPE.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick KANN over tiny-ml-runtime when you need training and RNNs rather than inference of a fixed tiny MLP, and over PyTorch, MXNet or Caffe when a dependency-free C source drop matters more than speed on big models or GPUs. Adept-2, XAD and CoDiPack are scalar operator-overloading AD for C++ numerical code, not neural-network training, so they rarely compete with KANN.
verified_claims_summary: First-party 2017 README table, one run per row on 2x Xeon E5-2697 2.7GHz (Linux) and a Core i7-3667U (Mac), compiler and flags unstated (the Makefile defaults to gcc -O2): mnist-mlp, 20 epochs, 1 thread, took 31.3 s for KANN with SSE and 18.8 s with OpenBLAS 0.2.19 versus 33.7 s for Theano 0.8.2 + Keras 1.2.2 with MKL and 2m19s for tiny-dnn, and with 4 threads KANN beat Theano+Keras on mnist-cnn (19m09s vs 24m24s) and mul100-rnn (12m13s, or 8m18s with OpenBLAS, vs 19m52s). Single-threaded without BLAS it lost to Theano+Keras on mnist-cnn (57m57s vs 37m12s) and mul100-rnn (40m05s vs 27m30s), and the baselines are 2017 releases, so the result is about framework overhead and threading on tiny models, not about KANN's kernels beating MKL.
status_note: Stale: commits stopped in April 2021 apart from two in June 2025 (NEON support, an mt-mode API), with 2019-2021 bug reports unanswered, but it is MIT-licensed, about 3,900 lines in four C files with no required dependencies, and easy to vendor and patch.
